c.tagline: Sicily's sun-baked capital, where Arab-Norman splendour meets raucous street-food markets.

taxi.fareNote: Official taxis are white and metered, though a fixed fare of around €45 applies from the airport to the centre. Uber offers only its licensed taxi/black-car service in Palermo (no UberX), so hailing at a rank or booking through Free Now or the itTaxi/appTaxi apps is the norm; agree the fare before longer rides.

emergency.note: 112 is the EU-wide emergency number connecting to police, fire, and ambulance; 113 reaches state police and 118 reaches medical emergencies directly.

avoid.reason: Pickpocketing/scooter bag-snatching in the markets (Ballarò, Vucciria); caution at night

hood_desc: The dense historic core around the Quattro Canti, the Cathedral, and the Ballaro market, where Arab-Norman monuments, baroque churches, and street-food stalls sit side by side; best for first-timers who want the sights and the buzz within walking distance.

A once-faded seaside quarter reborn as Palermo's arty heart, with the Foro Italico promenade, Palazzo Abatellis, lively piazzas, and a wave of galleries, cafes, and craft-cocktail bars; suits travellers after character and an evening scene.

Home to the atmospheric Vucciria market, sleepy by day and rowdy by night when its squares fill with students, street food, and open-air drinking; good for travellers who want to be in the thick of the nightlife.

The elegant modern centre around Teatro Politeama and the boutique-lined Via della Liberta, with grand 19th-century buildings, upscale shops, and reliable restaurants; suits those wanting a smarter, calmer base with easy transport.

Palermo's belle-epoque seaside resort about 20 minutes from the centre, with a crescent of white sand, art-nouveau villas, and seafood restaurants beneath Monte Pellegrino; ideal for a relaxed, beachy stay.

water.note: Tap water is officially safe, though most locals drink bottled for taste.

transit.hours: Buses and the four tram lines run roughly 5:30 AM to around midnight; a limited night bus network and taxis cover the late-night hours.
transit.note: AMAT runs the city buses and four modern tram lines (opened 2015), while Trenitalia's suburban 'passante ferroviario' rail links the main stations and the airport; buses remain the backbone for reaching most sights in the historic centre.
transit.pay: A single AMAT ticket is €1.40 and valid 90 minutes across buses and trams; a day pass is €3.50. Tickets are sold at tobacconists, newsstands, and machines, and contactless tap-and-go is being rolled out. Validate on board to avoid fines.

bus: Palermo Centrale / Piazzale Cairoli coach stops (Flixbus & intercity)

transit.m: Trinacria Express train to Palermo Centrale (~50 min, ~2/hour)
Prestia e Comande bus to city centre (~50 min, hourly)

tip.r: Not obligatory; a cover charge (coperto) is usually on the bill, so rounding up or leaving a euro or two for good service is appreciated but not expected.

food.name: Arancine
food.desc: Palermo's round fried rice balls - meat ragu and peas, or butter and ham - crisp outside, saffron rice within. Note the local feminine name.

places.name: Ke Palle
places.note: Central specialist frying a long list of arancine fillings all day.

places.name: Bar Touring
places.note: Old-school city-centre bar Palermitans rate for a classic carne arancina.

places.name: Antico Caffe Spinnato
places.note: Grand historic cafe with a polished version and outdoor tables.

food.name: Pane con la milza (pani ca meusa)
food.desc: The city's boldest street food: veal spleen and lung simmered in lard, piled into a sesame roll, schietto plain or maritato with ricotta and caciocavallo.

places.name: Antica Focacceria San Francesco
places.note: Serving it since 1834; the most famous milza counter in Sicily.

places.name: Nni Franco u Vastiddaru
places.note: Busy street counter near Porta Felice, open late for the classic roll.

places.name: Ballaro market stalls
places.note: Market carts serve the rawest, cheapest version to a local crowd.

food.name: Sfincione
food.desc: Spongy Palermo focaccia topped with onion, tomato, anchovy, oregano and breadcrumbs - sold from three-wheeler vans as much as from bakeries.

places.name: Panificio Morello
places.note: Bakery locals cross town for; sfincione sold by the tray slice.

places.name: Ballaro market vans
places.note: Sfincione hawkers work the market shouting their prices; buy it warm.

places.name: Vucciria stalls
places.note: Old market quarter with sfincione counters that run into the evening.

food.name: Panelle e crocche
food.desc: Chickpea-flour fritters and potato croquettes fried to order and stuffed into a soft sesame bun with lemon - the classic Palermo sandwich.

places.name: Friggitoria Chiluzzo
places.note: Neighbourhood friggitoria in the Kalsa, cheap and consistently praised.

places.name: Nni Franco u Vastiddaru
places.note: Reliable pane e panelle right on the main tourist axis.

places.name: Antica Focacceria San Francesco
places.note: Historic room where you can sit down with a panelle roll.

food.name: Stigghiola
food.desc: Lamb or kid intestines wound around spring onion and grilled over charcoal until charred, cut with scissors and hit with lemon and salt.

places.name: Ballaro evening grills
places.note: Charcoal braziers fire up as the market winds down; smoke marks the spot.

places.name: Vucciria night stalls
places.note: The quarter's late-night grills are the classic stigghiola experience.

places.name: Foro Italico kiosks
places.note: Seafront grills popular with local families on summer evenings.

food.name: Cannoli and Sicilian pastry
food.desc: Shells fried and filled to order with sheep's-milk ricotta, plus cassata, frutta martorana and convent sweets from the old monastery recipes.

places.name: Pasticceria Cappello
places.note: Family pastry shop famous for its setteveli cake as well as cannoli.

places.name: I Segreti del Chiostro
places.note: Inside Santa Caterina monastery, reviving nuns' recipes; cannoli filled on order.

places.name: Antico Caffe Spinnato
places.note: Historic cafe with a full counter of Sicilian pastry and ice cream.

food.name: Sicilian wine and Marsala
food.desc: Nero d'Avola, Etna reds and crisp Grillo whites, plus fortified Marsala from the west of the island poured as an aperitivo or dessert wine.

places.name: Enoteca Picone
places.note: Institution since 1946: shelves of Sicilian bottles and a standing wine bar.

places.name: Vucciria wine bars
places.note: Cheap glasses of local wine in the market's evening street-drinking scene.

places.name: Antica Focacceria San Francesco
places.note: Sicilian-only list to drink with the street-food menu.

food.name: Granita con brioche and caffe
food.desc: Sicilian breakfast: lemon, almond, coffee or mulberry granita spooned into a brioche col tuppo, with an espresso alongside.

places.name: Antico Caffe Spinnato
places.note: Trading since 1860; granita and brioche on a pedestrian street.

places.name: Bar Alba
places.note: Long-standing Palermo bar locals name first for granita and pastry.

places.name: Seafront kiosks at Mondello
places.note: Beach-suburb kiosks serve granita all summer, a short bus ride out.

landmarks: Palermo Cathedral
A magnificent architectural palimpsest of Norman, Gothic, Arabic and Baroque styles housing royal tombs, with rooftop walkways above its UNESCO-listed crowns and cupolas.
Palazzo dei Normanni & Cappella Palatina
Europe's oldest royal residence conceals the Palatine Chapel, a 12th-century jewel where Byzantine gold mosaics meet a carved Arab honeycomb ceiling.
Teatro Massimo
Italy's largest opera house, a neoclassical colossus of 1897 with legendary acoustics, immortalized in the final scenes of The Godfather Part III.
Quattro Canti
The theatrical Baroque crossroads dividing the old city into quarters, its four concave facades stacked with fountains, Spanish kings and patron saints.
Fontana Pretoria
A grandiose 16th-century Florentine fountain crowded with marble nudes, so scandalous to convent neighbors it earned the nickname 'Fountain of Shame.'
La Martorana (Santa Maria dell'Ammiraglio)
A 12th-century church glowing with some of Sicily's finest Byzantine mosaics, including a famous panel of Roger II crowned by Christ.
Catacombe dei Cappuccini (Capuchin Catacombs)
An eerily fascinating crypt where thousands of mummified Palermitans in period dress line the corridors, including the hauntingly preserved child Rosalia Lombardo.
Ballarò Market
Palermo's oldest street market, a raucous Arab-rooted theater of shouted 'abbanniate,' sizzling panelle and pyramids of swordfish, citrus and olives.
Monreale Cathedral
A short bus ride uphill, this Norman cathedral dazzles with 6,000 square meters of golden mosaics and a cloister of carved twin columns.
Mondello Beach
Palermo's Liberty-era seaside playground, a half-moon of white sand and turquoise shallows framed by Monte Pellegrino and a whimsical Art Nouveau pier.

train.note: Palermo has no international trains. Trenitalia runs regional services across Sicily from Palermo Centrale (Cefalu ~45 min, Agrigento ~2h, Catania ~3h) plus long-distance Intercity trains to the mainland that cross the Strait of Messina by rail ferry toward Naples and Rome.

bus.note: Coaches use the stops around Palermo Centrale and Piazzale Cairoli. Flixbus, SAIS, and Cuffaro run frequent services to Catania, Agrigento, Trapani, and other Sicilian towns, plus long-distance links to the mainland via the Messina ferry.

ferry.note: The Port of Palermo is a major ferry hub. Overnight car ferries sail to Naples, Genoa, Cagliari, and Livorno (GNV and Grimaldi Lines), a weekly line runs to Tunis, and hydrofoils serve the island of Ustica.

half.name: Cefalù
half.blurb: A Norman cathedral town with a sandy beach beneath a limestone crag sits about an hour east of Palermo.

half.name: Segesta
half.blurb: A remarkably intact ancient Greek temple and hilltop theater lie roughly an hour southwest of Palermo.

half.name: Erice
half.blurb: A medieval hilltop town with sweeping views of the Tyrrhenian coast is about ninety minutes from Palermo.

half.name: Zingaro Nature Reserve
half.blurb: A protected coastal park with hiking trails and secluded coves lies about an hour west of Palermo.
